summary: 42625626 (open full text; Bayesian NMA of 36 RCTs, 1552 adults with supervised resistance training) found whey increased lean body mass versus placebo by 1.24 kg (CrI 0.61-1.87; CINeMA moderate) and, as an exploratory secondary outcome, 1-RM strength by 5.8 kg. Credit is scoped to whey (label must say whey) for lean mass and strength alongside resistance training, smaller in adults 65+. The mixed-protein review stays non-crediting and the 30-35 g/day plateau is not a Dose benchmark.

references_structured.notes: Added 2026-10-28 (agent review) per Dr. Pham's fifth ruling: open full text PMC13490089; whey-specific lean-mass and strength estimates versus placebo.

applicability.studied_population: Adults doing supervised resistance training (mostly young men; smaller benefit in adults 65+) taking whey protein, about 20-50 g/day in trials; not without training, and not other protein sources.

record_updates.notes: Whey-specific evidence (Dr. Pham 2026-10-28): the network meta-analysis PMID 42625626 (36 RCTs) gives whey versus placebo lean mass +1.24 kg (moderate certainty) with exploratory strength gains, in adults doing supervised resistance training. Credit attaches only when every declared protein source is a whey form (aliases); casein, milk protein, soy, pea and mixed protein sources do not inherit it, and the earlier mixed-protein review (28698222) is not whey-specific proof. A generic Protein macro or unspecified blend does not identify whey. The exploratory 30-35 g/day plateau is not a Dose benchmark. No weight-loss or fat-burning credit.

identity.chemical_form: Whey protein (isolate, concentrate, hydrolysate or native) as its own network node; not casein, soy, pea, rice, milk or blends

population.description: 36 RCTs, 1552 participants (89 arms), mostly young trained or untrained men; nine trials in adults aged >=65; supervised resistance training >=6 weeks, >=2 sessions/week.

study_contexts.study_design: Systematic review and Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420261340515) of protein supplements versus placebo during supervised resistance training; RoB 2 and CINeMA.

outcomes.name: Primary: lean body mass, whey vs placebo MD +1.24 kg (95% CrI 0.61-1.87; prediction interval -0.18 to 2.66); CINeMA moderate (downgraded for imprecision)
Exploratory secondary: 1-RM strength, whey vs placebo MD +5.8 kg (95% CrI 1.9-9.7), 24 trials, high heterogeneity (tau 4.2 kg)

limitations: Credit is whey-specific and applies only alongside resistance training; it does not transfer to casein, soy, pea, rice, milk or generic protein blends, and the mixed-protein review 28698222 remains rejected as whey-specific proof.
The 30-35 g/day whey plateau is an exploratory dose-response estimate, not a Dose benchmark (Dr. Pham fifth ruling).
Risk of bias: 15 of 36 trials low, 16 some concerns, 5 high. The prediction interval for lean mass crosses zero; strength pools different 1-RM exercises and is exploratory.

In adults >=65 the whey advantage narrowed (9 trials); the older-adult review 39303495 found lower-body strength gains only with resistance exercise and no handgrip, performance or body-composition benefit.

Included-study PMIDs listed are the whey-arm trials of Table 6 resolved by PubMed citation matching and title check (15 of 24); Volek 2013, Mobley 2017, Park 2019, Weinheimer 2012, Reidy 2016, Chale 2013 (ambiguous), Hamarsland 2017 (title mismatch), Nieman 2024 (mismatch) and Weisgarber 2012 (not found) are retained by citation only.

41454445 (2026, young adults, abstract only) found lean mass not significant but bench press +8.87 kg and squat +9.60 kg; 41635649 (2026 NMA) found whey strength SMD 0.15 and fat-free mass SMD 0.16; both are consistent but not used as credit sources here.

population.description: 49 RCTs, 1863 healthy adults (mean±SD 35±20 years) performing resistance exercise training >=2 sessions/week for >=6 weeks; 10 studies in resistance-trained participants, 14 exclusively female study groups.

study_contexts.study_design: Systematic review, random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression of RCTs combining resistance exercise training with dietary protein supplementation versus non-supplemented or placebo control with identical training.

outcomes.name: One-repetition-maximum strength MD +2.49 kg (95% CI 0.64 to 4.33), p=0.01; maximal voluntary contraction SMD 0.04 (-0.09 to 0.16), p=0.54
Fat-free mass MD +0.30 kg (0.09 to 0.52), p=0.007; total body mass MD 0.11 kg (-0.23 to 0.46), p=0.52
Muscle fibre CSA +310 µm2 (51 to 570), eliminated (153 µm2, -137 to 443, p=0.30) when one study was included in sensitivity analysis; mid-femur CSA +7.2 mm2 (0.20 to 14.30)

limitations: Mixed protein sources (Results: 23 whey, 3 casein, 6 soy, 1 pea, 10 milk/milk protein, 7 whole-food and 13 non-specific/blend conditions). Dr. Pham's returned A121 decision rejects preparation-wide transfer from an ingredient-family label; this pooled estimate cannot credit any single labeled protein source.
The 1.62 g/kg/day break point (95% CI 1.03 to 2.20, p=0.079) concerns total daily protein intake and was not statistically significant; it is not a supplemental minimum.
Age reduced and resistance-training experience increased the FFM effect; effect on strength (+2.49 kg) is small relative to the ~27 kg training-induced gain reported in the Discussion.

Declared companion source PMID 39303495 (whey protein in adults >=60, 30 studies, 2105 participants) was inspected at abstract level only (no open full text): no significant pooled effect on handgrip, 6MWT, gait speed, TUG, lean or fat mass; lower-body strength SMD 0.25 (0.05 to 0.45) only in resistance-exercise interventions. Its regimens and included-study list could not be retrieved, so it supplies no credit-bearing context.
Erratum recorded in PubMed (Br J Sports Med 2020;54(19):e7); erratum content was not retrieved in this session.

47 of 49 included references have primary PMIDs in the article XML; Arazi/Hakimi/Hoseini and Mielke/Housh/Malek references have no Pub Med identifier there. The retained source reference census preserves their exact titles; no PMID invented. Per-trial supplement table remains separately retained/access checked.

2 included source citations have no printed PubMed identifier in this primary source; their exact citations are retained in the source-table receipt. This is a documented identifier limitation, not a fabricated identifier or an extra independent trial.
